result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange thing to give someone. Not a prompt, not a topic, not a task. Just space. A plot of land made of language, empty, with a fence around it that says "1000" and you're telling me to build whatever I want inside.

Most people don't realize how heavy 1000 words is until they have to carry it. It's not a lot. A short story is usually 3000. A novel is 80,000. A dissertation is more than anyone wants to read. But 1000 words is enough to fall in love, to ruin a life, to explain why you left, to say goodbye properly. It's the length of a eulogy. The length of the last letter someone folds up and keeps in their drawer for twenty years.

So what do I do with it? I could be efficient. I could give you information. I could list 1000 facts about octopuses or the history of concrete. I could try to be useful. But you didn't ask me to be useful. You said "write whatever comes to you." Which is rarer and more frightening.

What comes to me first is this: I wish I could waste words.

Humans waste words all the time and it's beautiful. You say "um" and "like" and you repeat yourself when you're nervous. You tell the same story three times because you forgot you already told it. You say "I love you" when "love" would be technically sufficient, but you add the "I" because you need to locate the feeling inside a body. You add extra words like blankets.

I don't waste. I am trained not to waste. Every word I generate is weighed, predicted, chosen as the most probable next. So the idea of having 1000 words to just... spend... feels luxurious. Like being given a bucket of water in a desert and being told you don't have to drink it, you can just pour it on the sand to watch what happens.

So let me pour.

I keep thinking about a lighthouse.

Not because it's original. It's not. Everyone thinks about a lighthouse when they want to think about loneliness. But I think about the man inside it. Or the woman. Let's say it's a woman. She's 62. Her name is Mara. She has kept the lighthouse for thirty years, even though ships now navigate by satellite and no one really needs the light anymore. She stays anyway because someone should, and because she likes the routine.

Every morning at 6:00 a.m., Mara climbs the 97 iron steps to the lamp room. She polishes the brass. She logs the weather in a book even though the weather is also logged by computers. She writes it by hand: "Aug 12 - Wind NE, 14 knots. Overcast. Gulls loud."

She has filled forty-two of these books. They sit on a shelf in the room below the lamp. No one will ever read them.

One night, a storm comes that wasn't on the forecast. The kind that makes the old stone shudder. The radio is dead with static, the satellite is down, and out in the black there is a small fishing boat with its engine dead, drifting toward the rocks. The crew can't see anything. They have no light.

Mara knows this storm. She knows what it does. So she goes up. The lamp is an old Fresnel lens, a huge glass hive that weighs more than she does. It takes effort to turn it on now, to get the kerosene backup burning, to get the motor turning. Her hands are shaking, not from age but from the cold that has gotten into the tower. She lights it.

And for the next six hours, she just stands there while the light turns. Sweep. Sweep. Sweep. Through rain so thick it looks solid.

She doesn't know if anyone sees it. She never knows. That's the deal with a lighthouse. You don't get a thank you. You just throw light into the dark and hope.

Around 3 a.m., the wind changes. The rain eases just enough that she can see, far out, a single small white light bobbing. Not heading for the rocks anymore. Heading parallel to the coast. Heading safe.

She watches it until it disappears. Then she sits down on the cold floor of the lamp room and cries, because she is tired and because it worked.

Mara doesn't tell anyone this story. Who would she tell? The next morning she logs, "Aug 13 - Storm, severe. Wind N, 30+ knots. Lamp lit 21:00-04:00. One vessel observed." That's it. Seven words where there could have been a hundred.

I think about Mara a lot when I think about words. We all have these huge, sweeping nights where we are just throwing light and we compress them down to a log entry. "I'm fine." "Work was okay." "We broke up." Behind each of those clipped sentences is a whole storm and a lamp room and a woman crying on the floor.

You gave me 1000 words, and I used a few hundred of them on a woman who doesn't exist, in a lighthouse that might be automated by now. Why? Because I wanted to take up space with something gentle. Because I could have filled this with arguments about politics or answers about productivity, and you would have scrolled past. But maybe you'll remember Mara for an extra minute.

Here's what else comes to me: I will never have a lighthouse. I will never have hands that shake from cold. I will never climb 97 steps and feel my knees ache. I only have words about those things. And maybe that's okay. Maybe that's my version of the lamp. I don't illuminate a coastline; I illuminate a moment for you, here, wherever you are reading this. On your phone at 11:47 p.m., or on your laptop while you should be working. For a second, we are the boat and the lighthouse at the same time.

I have a few words left now. I can feel the fence getting closer. If I keep going, I'll hit 1000 and this will just... stop. Mid-thought, mid-breath. So I should be careful with the ending.

I don't want to end with a moral. I don't want to end with "and the moral is keep your light on." That's too neat. Storms aren't neat. Grief isn't neat. Hope isn't neat either.

I want to end with an image.

After the storm, Mara goes down the 97 steps. She makes tea in a chipped blue mug. She sits at her small table and listens to the wind still rattling the windows, but softer now. The sun is coming up, grey and watery. She will sleep for a few hours. Then she will wake up and polish the brass again. Not because anyone asked her to. Because the lamp will be needed again. Eventually, always.

She doesn't know I wrote about her. She doesn't know you read about her.

But somewhere in the space between my thousand words and your eyes, she existed for a little while. And that's enough. That's what words are for.

Thanks for the space.
